prompt.context: Your client is Tacotle, a leading national fast casual restaurant with $420m in revenue in 2019. Over the five years preceding 2019, Tacotle has experienced steady revenue growth and industry leading profitability. But for the first time in its 15 year history, Tacotle has experienced three straight quarters of EBITDA erosion. Tacotle's CEO has hired you to explore what is causing profits to drop and what can be done to reverse the tide.
prompt.question: What is causing Tacotle's profits to drop, and what can be done to reverse the trend?

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific profitability target we need to hit?
clarifying_info.a: No specific milestones — the goal is positive annual profit growth in the short term.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization — think of it as operating profit.

clarifying_info.q: Can you tell me about the market or competitive landscape?
clarifying_info.a: Defer this until after you present your framework.

exhibits.title: Quarterly Revenue and EBITDA
exhibits.shows: A dual-series bar/line chart plotting quarterly Revenue ($M) and EBITDA ($M) from Q1 2012 through Q4 2019, with EBITDA % margin labels for recent quarters

data.notes: Revenue spikes sharply in Q1 2019 then declines; EBITDA remains relatively flat while EBITDA% drops ~5-6 pts in 2019

exhibits.title: Average Revenue per Order
exhibits.shows: A line chart of average revenue per order (y-axis $3.00–$5.50) from Q1 2017 through Q4 2019

data.notes: Price rises sharply at the start of 2019 and stays elevated through the year

exhibits.title: Income Statement 2017–2019
exhibits.shows: A three-year income statement (2017, 2018, 2019) showing Revenue, COGS, Wages, SG&A, Fixed Overhead, and EBITDA

exhibits.title: Customer Survey 2018
exhibits.shows: A horizontal bar chart comparing Importance vs. Performance ratings (scale 0–5) across seven attributes for 2018

data.performance_scores: not shown separately in raw text — chart bars indicate Tacotle lags on Quality, meets or exceeds others

exhibits.title: Customer Survey 2019
exhibits.shows: A horizontal bar chart comparing Importance vs. Performance ratings (scale 0–5) across seven attributes for 2019 — same survey repeated one year later

data.notes: Attribute order has changed vs 2018; Speed of Service is now listed first

framework: Profit = Revenue – Costs; start by splitting EBITDA erosion into a revenue problem vs. a cost problem
Revenue side: break into Price x Quantity; check whether avg order price changed and whether unit volume changed
Cost side: split into fixed costs (PP&E, SG&A, Marketing) vs. variable costs (COGS, Distribution, Labor); identify which line items moved
External market check: GDP-level market growth, competitive entry/exit, new substitutes, market share stability, shifts in customer preferences
Operations: if costs or revenue moved, link back to an operational/strategic change inside Tacotle (e.g., product mix change, menu redesign, sourcing change)

questions.prompt: Step 2 — What do external market conditions tell us about the source of Tacotle's profit problem?
questions.guidance: Candidate should proactively ask about market growth, competition, and customers. Key takeaways: market grows at GDP pace (mature); no major competitor entry/exit; no new substitutes; Tacotle holds 30% market share. Conclusion: the problem is not market-wide — it is Tacotle-specific. Customer preferences are shifting toward ingredient quality and order customization, which may have influenced internal decisions.

questions.prompt: Step 3 — Using Exhibit A, what trends do you observe in revenue and EBITDA, and what hypotheses does that generate?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies: (1) sharp revenue spike in Q1 2019 followed by steady decline, (2) EBITDA stays nearly flat ($169M vs $170M) despite revenue jumping to $420M, (3) EBITDA% drops ~5-6 percentage points in 2019 vs 2018. Candidate should hypothesize that price and/or quantity increased but costs rose disproportionately, or that the revenue spike attracted costs that didn't scale back when revenue fell.

questions.prompt: Step 4 — Using Exhibit B, what drove the revenue increase in 2019?
questions.guidance: Candidate should quickly identify that average price per order rose sharply at the start of 2019 (from ~$4.05 to ~$5.25). They should then flag the ambiguity: higher price could accompany higher OR lower unit volume — do not jump to conclusions. The next step is to calculate units sold to resolve this.

questions.prompt: Step 5 — Using Exhibit C, calculate the change in units sold between 2018 and 2019.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up Units Sold = Revenue / Avg Price Per Unit for each year, round inputs to clean numbers, and interpret the result. Although revenue increased, units sold actually fell — meaning the price increase did not attract more customers. The continued quarterly revenue decline post-Q1 2019 at a stable price confirms that declining unit volume is driving EBITDA erosion.

math.setup: Units Sold = Revenue / Average Price Per Unit
steps: 2018: Revenue = $377M, round to $380M; Avg price = $4.05, round to $4.00
math.answer: Units sold fell from ~95M in 2018 to ~80M in 2019, a decrease of ~15M units (~16%) despite the revenue increase.

questions.prompt: Step 6a — Using Exhibit D (2018 customer survey), why might Tacotle have raised prices, and what operational change likely drove it?
questions.guidance: Exhibit D shows Tacotle lagged on Quality (the highest-importance attribute) in 2018. A strong candidate infers that Tacotle undertook a quality-improvement initiative — likely a menu overhaul with higher-quality or more-customizable ingredients — which caused COGS to nearly double ($54M to $96M) and required a price increase to partially offset. The interviewer should confirm: Tacotle introduced a new menu focused on ingredient quality and order customization.

questions.prompt: Step 6b — Using Exhibit E (2019 customer survey), did the menu change succeed? What happened to customer satisfaction?
questions.guidance: Exhibit E shows the same survey one year later. Key observations: (1) 'Speed of Service' is now ranked #1 in importance but Tacotle's performance appears weakest there — the new complex menu slowed service from ~1 min to ~3.5 min; (2) 'Consistency of Product' also dropped below expectations due to added preparation complexity; (3) Although 'Quality' improved to meet expectations, the drop in Speed and Consistency more than cancelled the gain, resulting in net customer dissatisfaction. This explains the quarter-over-quarter decline in units sold.

brainstorming.prompt: What operational risks or unintended consequences should Tacotle consider when scaling back the menu changes?

categories.name: Customer Experience
ideas: Reverting quality improvements may disappoint customers who valued the upgrade
Inconsistent rollback messaging could confuse loyal customers
Loss of customization options may alienate a newly acquired segment

categories.name: Operations
ideas: Simplified menu reduces prep complexity and restores service speed
Fewer SKUs lower staff training burden and reduce error rates
Consistency of product likely recovers as complexity decreases

categories.name: Supply Chain & Costs
ideas: Scaling back may strain or terminate supplier relationships built for the new menu
Asset divestiture may be needed for equipment purchased for the menu upgrade
Renegotiating supply contracts could take time and incur penalties

categories.name: Financial
ideas: A scale-back that doesn't cut costs proportionally could shrink both revenue and profits
If prices are also reduced, revenue per order falls further
Need to ensure COGS savings exceed any revenue loss from price reductions

recommendation: Scale back the menu changes introduced in 2019: reduce ingredient complexity and return to a simpler, faster menu to restore Speed of Service and product Consistency
Maintain selective quality improvements (e.g., one or two premium options) to protect gains in the Quality attribute without sacrificing operational throughput
risks: Scaling back too aggressively could erode the Quality rating Tacotle worked to improve, undoing brand-equity gains
Reverting may damage supplier relationships or require costly contract adjustments and asset write-downs
A rollback that does not also address pricing and cost structure could shrink revenue and profits simultaneously, effectively downsizing the company
next_steps: Conduct more detailed and targeted customer surveys to understand exactly which menu elements drive satisfaction vs. dissatisfaction
Execute a disciplined menu reduction focused on cost-cutting balanced against customer priorities
Pilot future menu changes at a small number of individual restaurants before national rollout to reduce execution risk
